vignette:
She arrives to each session with clay under her fingernails, a detail she noticed me noticing once and now seems to use as a quiet offering before she speaks. She is sixty-one, her hands quick and strong, the kind of hands that have spent decades coaxing form out of wet earth. But in the past year, those hands have begun to shake when she reaches for her tools.

The event happened six years ago, though she tells it as if it were last Tuesday. She was driving home from a small gallery opening—her own work, a series of abstract torsos—when she saw the boy run out between two parked cars. She remembers the sound of the impact as something between a crack and a silence, a thing she cannot describe but has heard every night since. She was the first to reach him. She held his hand while someone else called for help. He was eight years old. He did not survive.

She did not know the boy. She did not know his family. In the months that followed, she attended the funeral, left food at the door, and eventually stopped. People told her she had done everything right, that she was a good person for staying. But she tells me now that she has never believed that. She stayed because she could not move. She held his hand because she had no idea what else to do. And that, she says, is the terrible truth: she did nothing heroic, she simply froze.

For the first two years, she kept working. She sculpted a series of small, smooth figures—children, she says now, though she did not see it at the time. She gave them away. She did not keep photographs. Her husband noticed she stopped listening to music in the car. She started taking the long way home, the route that avoided that intersection, even if it added twenty minutes. She told herself it was for the scenery.

But the avoidance grew. She stopped driving at night. Then she stopped driving alone. Then she stopped driving at all, unless her husband was beside her. He drives her to the studio now. She sits in the passenger seat, her eyes fixed straight ahead, her hands gripping her own thighs. She has not told him why.

In the studio, she finds it harder to begin. The clay feels cold in a way it never did. She will stand at the worktable for ten, twenty minutes, staring at a block she has already wedged, unable to make the first cut. When she does begin, it is often with too much force, and the piece collapses. She used to work on four or five sculptures at once. Now she works on one, and she works slowly, sanding edges long after they are smooth. She has not started a new piece in three months.

Sleep comes in fragments. She wakes at three in the morning with the sound of the impact in her chest, her husband snoring beside her. She lies still, afraid to move, afraid to wake him. Some nights she gets up and goes to the studio in her house, where she keeps a small lamp on at all times—she cannot work in the dark anymore. She sits in the chair by the window and waits for morning.

She avoids children. This is the hardest thing to say, and she almost does not say it. But one afternoon, in a low voice, she tells me she crossed the street to avoid a school group last month. She saw the small bodies in bright jackets, and she felt a pressure in her throat, a physical panic. She turned and walked the other way. She felt shame, hot and immediate, and that shame has stayed.

She still uses her hands. She still makes things. But the work has changed—the forms are more closed, more inward. She has not shown anything since that gallery opening. Her husband asks when she will have a new exhibition, and she says soon, though she does not know if she means it.

Today, she is wearing a sweater with traces of dried clay on the sleeve. She looks at the floor and says she does not know if she is getting better or worse. She is here, though. She keeps coming. And that, perhaps, is the only thing she still trusts.
